idea: A huge interrobang (‽) drawn as a clean specimen glyph, with small text below: 'Interrobang. Martin K. Speckter, 1962. Still waiting for its moment‽' It's for people who love punctuation as design: a real mark, invented by an ad man, that never quite caught on.

A long s (ſ) and an f side by side at display size, with the missing crossbar circled and the caption 'ſ is not f. Retired c. 1800.' It shows the reader the trick for reading old books, which is the kind of quiet expertise these customers like to wear.

The alphabet A to Z in a classic specimen grid, with a 27th square holding a large italic ampersand labelled 'and per se and'. Schoolchildren once recited & as the last letter of the alphabet, and that phrase was slurred into the word 'ampersand'.

One large pilcrow (¶) floating beside an empty indented line, captioned 'The indent is where this used to go.' Scribes left gaps for rubricators to paint in paragraph marks, which often never got added, so the blank indent became the convention. It's a smart reveal about something people see every day.

'Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet' set like a quiet book page, with a footnote reading 'Scrambled Cicero, 45 BC. The original is about pain.' Every designer knows the filler text, but few know that it comes from De finibus, from a line about not loving pain for its own sake ('dolorem ipsum').

A short vertical line of Ogham strokes on a stem line, with a key underneath and the caption 'Ogham. Early medieval Ireland. Written up the edge of a stone.' It's a stark, beautiful geometric alphabet, and the angle is that some writing was cut into corners instead of onto flat surfaces.

Wedge-pressed proto-cuneiform signs and tally marks in tidy rows, with the line 'The first writing was a receipt.' The earliest tablets from Uruk are mostly administrative records of grain, beer and livestock, so it's a dry, true punchline about where literature came from.

Hangul's five basic consonants (ㄱ ㄴ ㅁ ㅅ ㅇ), each next to a small profile diagram of the mouth or throat shape it depicts, captioned 'Hangul, 1443. An alphabet drawn from the mouth that speaks it.' King Sejong's script really was designed this way, and it's one of the most elegant ideas in the history of writing.

A single oversized semicolon in an Aldine-style roman, with 'Venice, 1490s. A pause that isn't quite a stop.' Aldus Manutius's press popularised the semicolon in print, and wearing the mark that refuses to end a sentence says something about the wearer.

A line diagram of a compositor's job case, every compartment filled with its metal letter, with the upper and lower cases labelled and the caption 'Upper case. Lower case. It was furniture first.' The terms come from the physical cases printers kept capitals and small letters in, which is a lovely etymology to wear.

The hieroglyphic cartouche of Ptolemy as it appears on the Rosetta Stone, with 'Champollion started with a name.' Deciphering the cartouche was a key step to reading Egyptian, and the shirt turns a famous breakthrough into one quiet, graphic object.

'HERE MEN FROM THE PLANET EARTH FIRST SET FOOT UPON THE MOON JULY 1969, A.D. WE CAME IN PEACE FOR ALL MANKIND' in Futura capitals, with a tiny note: 'Set in Futura (Paul Renner, 1927).' The Apollo 11 plaque really was set in Futura, so a typeface from Weimar Germany is sitting on the Moon.

A line of Voynich-manuscript-style glyphs, redrawn as clean type, with 'Vellum dated to the early 1400s. Still unread.' It's beautiful, mysterious lettering with a point of view: writing can survive longer than our ability to read it.

The word 'minuscule' written in Carolingian minuscule, captioned 'Lowercase: a 9th-century Frankish book hand the Renaissance mistook for ancient Rome.' Humanist scribes copied Carolingian manuscripts believing they were classical, and their copies became our lowercase. The best typographic origin stories are mistakes.

'SENATVS POPVLVSQVE ROMANVS' in Roman square capitals based on the Trajan's Column inscription, with 'AD 113. No J, no U, no W.' These are the letterforms behind nearly every serif capital, and the caption reminds the wearer that the alphabet is still being edited.

The word READ in large Braille cells drawn as solid dots, with 'Louis Braille was 15. He adapted an artillery captain's system for reading without light.' It's a graphic, minimal design with a true and moving story about a teenager rebuilding someone else's idea into an alphabet.

The title characters of the Jikji (直指) in bold brush-like strokes, with '1377. Printed in movable metal type, 78 years before Gutenberg's Bible.' The Jikji, printed in Korea, is the oldest surviving book printed with movable metal type, which quietly corrects the usual Western story.

'ETAOIN SHRDLU' cast as a Linotype slug, slightly crooked, with 'Linotype operators ran a finger down the keys to kill a bad line. Sometimes it got printed anyway.' Those are the first two columns of the Linotype keyboard, sorted by letter frequency, and the phrase is a ghost that turned up in real newspapers.

A left-to-right sequence showing an ox-head pictogram turning into Phoenician aleph, Greek alpha and Latin A, captioned 'A is an ox, turned over.' Our first letter began as a picture of an ox's head, and seeing it rotate across 3,000 years is both beautiful and clever.

A big Tironian et (⁊) with 'Shorthand for "and" credited to Cicero's secretary Tiro. Still on Irish road signs.' It's an obscure, striking glyph with a 2,000-year working life: it stands for 'agus' on bilingual signs in Ireland today.
